import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 366

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/366](https://www.erdosproblems.com/366)
-/

namespace Erdos366

/--
Are there any $2$-full $n$ such that $n+1$ is $3$-full?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_366 : answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ n > 0, (2).Full n ∧ (3).Full (n + 1) := by
  sorry

/--
Note that $8$ is $3$-full and $9$ is 2-full.
-/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem exists_three_full_then_two_full : ∃ n > 0, (3).Full n ∧ (2).Full (n + 1) := by
  use 8
  norm_num +contextual [Nat.Full, Nat.primeFactors, Nat.primeFactorsList]

/--
Are there infinitely many 3-full $n$ such that $n+1$ is 2-full?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_366.variants.three_two :
    answer(sorry) ↔ {n | (3).Full n ∧ (2).Full (n + 1)}.Infinite := by
  sorry

/--
Are there any consecutive pairs of $3$-full integers?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_366.variants.weaker : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∃ n > 0, (3).Full n ∧ (3).Full (n + 1) := by
  sorry


end Erdos366

findings.description: The declaration asks whether there are infinitely many 3-full n with n+1 2-full. The cited reverse-order question instead asks whether n=8 is the only positive solution. Infinitude is stronger than the existence of an additional pair and is not a reformulation of the uniqueness question. The source's negative answer to uniqueness is certified by the single additional pair (12167,12168); it does not settle infinitude. I verified this pair and refuted the uniqueness proposition in Lean without using the file's sorry-backed theorems.
findings.source_evidence: Erdős and Graham, Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory (1980), p.68, asks: “Is n = 8 the only solution for B₃(n) = n, B₂(n+1) = n+1?” Here B_k(n)=n expresses k-fullness. Author-hosted scan: https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~ronspubs/80_11_number_theory.pdf (PDF page 64). The current https://www.erdosproblems.com/latex/366 likewise says “Erdős and Graham asked if this is the only pair of such consecutive integers,” and supplies 12167=23³ and 12168=2³·3²·13² as another example.
findings.suggested_fix: State the cited uniqueness question as `answer(False) ↔ ∀ n > 0, (3).Full n ∧ (2).Full (n + 1) → n = 8`, update the docstring accordingly, and mark that corrected statement `research solved`. This proposition was proved in the scratch file using n=12167. If the infinitude question is intentionally retained as an additional variant, give it separate sourcing rather than substituting it for the cited uniqueness question.

reformulations.difference: The infinitude statement ranges over all naturals, including zero, rather than explicitly restricting n to positive integers.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: This boundary choice is harmless independently of the source-question mismatch above. Removing zero removes at most one element, so `{n | (3).Full n ∧ (2).Full (n+1)}.Infinite` is equivalent to `{n | 0 < n ∧ (3).Full n ∧ (2).Full (n+1)}.Infinite`. The scratch file proves the general equivalence `{n | P n}.Infinite ↔ {n | 0 < n ∧ P n}.Infinite` by deleting the finite singleton {0}.

sources_consulted: P. Erdős and R. L. Graham, Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number theory (1980), pp.67–69; https://mathweb.ucsd.edu/~ronspubs/80_11_number_theory.pdf
P. Erdős, Problems and results on number theoretic properties of consecutive integers and related questions (1976), especially p.31; https://www.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1976-39.pdf
Local checkout: STATEMENTS.md, CONTRIBUTING.md, and AGENTS.md.
Supplied calibration material: /workspace/past_misformalizations/INDEX.md; pr04675.md, pr01138.md, pr01195.md, pr01406.md, pr03884.md, and pr04103.md.

Updated the docstring and proved the negative answer using the pair (12167, 12168). No other declarations were changed. import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 366

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/366](https://www.erdosproblems.com/366)
-/

namespace Erdos366

/--
Are there any $2$-full $n$ such that $n+1$ is $3$-full?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_366 : answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ n > 0, (2).Full n ∧ (3).Full (n + 1) := by
  sorry

/--
Note that $8$ is $3$-full and $9$ is 2-full.
-/
@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem exists_three_full_then_two_full : ∃ n > 0, (3).Full n ∧ (2).Full (n + 1) := by
  use 8
  norm_num +contextual [Nat.Full, Nat.primeFactors, Nat.primeFactorsList]

/--
Is $8$ the only positive $3$-full integer $n$ such that $n+1$ is $2$-full?

The answer is no: $12167 = 23^3$ and $12168 = 2^3 \cdot 3^2 \cdot 13^2$
form another such pair.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_366.variants.three_two :
    answer(False) ↔ ∀ n > 0, (3).Full n ∧ (2).Full (n + 1) → n = 8 := by
  constructor
  · exact False.elim
  · intro h
    have hpair : (3).Full 12167 ∧ (2).Full (12167 + 1) := by
      norm_num [Nat.Full, Nat.primeFactors, Nat.primeFactorsList]
    have h_eq := h 12167 (by norm_num) hpair
    norm_num at h_eq

/--
Are there any consecutive pairs of $3$-full integers?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_366.variants.weaker : answer(sorry) ↔
    ∃ n > 0, (3).Full n ∧ (3).Full (n + 1) := by
  sorry


end Erdos366
